newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond futures traded in a narrow range on Tuesday in a tense but relatively quiet session, dominated by speculation about the impact on monetary union of French calls for time to reflect on the stability pact, designed to keep spending of euro members under control.

Traders said the general view was that monetary union would still start on time in 1999, with a broad number of countries taking part, but that caution would prevail ahead of a Franco-German summit on June 13 and an EU summit in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17.
"People are wondering if Poitiers (Franco-German summit) and then Amsterdam will allow them to find an agreement," a futures trader at a French bank.
He said operators were cautious. "We'll probably have to wait for June 16 and 17" and until then the markets will continue to fluctuate in narrow ranges like today, he said.

An economist at a European bank said, "the stability pact is a problem without being a problem. It raises some uncertainty for the market but I'm still convinced that the Socialists will go ahead with the euro."

"The French have set their odds very high in order to get some words from the Germans - the only problem is how far they push them. If the (Germans) won't move...it could easily lead to disruption between Germany and France so the risk is there," he said. "In my view they are diplomatic enough, especially (Foreign Minister Hubert) Vedrine, to know how far they can go."
Another trader said, "Overall, the market believes so much in the succes of the euro, that there's only a risk of bad news. That's what worries me."

The 10-year spread between French and German yields narrowed slightly to minus six basis points from minus seven on Monday while the short end continued to bear the brunt of the pressure on the franc.

September PIBOR fell six basis points to 96.36 and the two-year spread over Germany widened to 30 basis points from 25, helping to shave another three basis points off the gap between two- and 10-year bonds.
A trader said he thought the 10-year OAT yield, at 5.72 percent on Tuesday, would remain stuck between 5.65 and 5.80 percent until after the Amsterdam summit.
"Domestics have the cash to invest, but really, caution is winning at the moment," he said.
The French franc slipped to a low of 3.3843 per mark, coming under pressure in the afternoon, from a low of 3.3795. It was trading at 3.3833 at 1547 GMT.
The Treasury announced it would be selling 300 million to 500 million Ecu of 5.5 percent 2007 and 6.75 percent 2002 OATs at its regular monthly auction on Thursday.
